newsitem.title: USA: N.J. says $2.8 bln pension bonds would save $1 bln.
newsitem.headline: N.J. says $2.8 bln pension bonds would save $1 bln.

text.p: New Jersey officials said Wednesday a proposed $2.8 billion pension obligation bond issue would save the state $1 billion over five years, a new estimate released on the eve of a touch-and-go vote on the deal by state lawmakers.

Mary Lou Murphy, a spokeswoman for Treasurer-designate James DiEleuterio, said DiEleuterio had met with rating agency officials late last week to relay the new estimates. Murphy said rating agency officials, who only last month warned that the deal could put New Jersey's ratings at risk, reacted favorably.
Murphy said officials at Standard & Poor's told the New Jersey delegation that if the deal's structure remained the same and the figures panned out, the state's AA-plus rating appeared secure.
Last month, S&P issued a statement warning that the pension bond deal, in conjunction with other budget problems, "may not be fully consistent with a AA-plus rating."

Glenn Goldberg, a managing director at Standard & Poor's Corp., said in an interview that the agency would offer another formal rating judgment only after the state completed its budget and the legislative process regarding the bond deal was complete.
He confirmed that the state had presented S&P with "more optimistic" fiscal projections, but said "it remains to be seen whether that view pans out."

Gov. Christine Whitman proposed the bond deal earlier this year to eliminate the state's unfunded pension liability. But the deal would also free up about $590 million in immediate budget savings, prompting criticism that the huge borrowing was merely a fiscal gimmick to pay for Whitman's income tax cuts.

Both the state Senate and Assembly have scheduled votes for Thursday on the bond deal, which Merrill Lynch & Co Inc would underwrite if approved. The vote might be delayed, as it was early this year, but a final budget must be approved by June 30.
Support for the bill remains thin, with several Republicans indicating they will join Democrats in voting it down.
